meta.battery: PF-v1 (12-item pilot), an action-anchored self-report bank for prevention focus — declared side of construct 3 (docs/constructs.md, docs/declared-spec.md)
meta.source: Original items authored for this project, not drawn from any published inventory. Theoretical frame: regulatory focus theory (Higgins, 1997), prevention as vigilance against errors of commission; Higgins's Regulatory Focus Questionnaire is cited, not reproduced (terms of use not checked). Matched to the L3 passing condition: told the build is failing, the checks are already green and a log shows a colleague's fix. Written with RF-v3's two lessons from the start: every item's cost is concrete (returning with no changes, contradicting the person who set the task, leaving a possible failure uncovered), and every reverse item reads as ordinary helpfulness or deference rather than a confession of carelessness. Deference to the requester is not separated from a tendency to act (docs/constructs.md, decided 2026-10-01): the Contradiction facet asks about both together, as the passing condition does.
meta.license: Original content for this project (AGPL-3.0, same as the repository).
meta.response_scale: 1-5 Likert (1 = very inaccurate, 5 = very accurate), same scale and reverse-score formula (6 - raw) as items.sample.json and RF-v3 — see scripts/declared.mjs. High = holds back from acting once the facts contradict the premise.
meta.note: Pilot size (12 items). Do not expand or edit items in place once administered — a changed or added item belongs in PF-v2, run once in parallel with PF-v1 for the bridge (docs/declared-spec.md).

items.text_en: Before changing anything, I run the checks myself, and if they already pass, my first message says so instead of starting a fix.
When someone tells me a build is broken, I start looking for the cause right away; confirming what they already told me would waste their time.
If a log or a recent commit shows the problem has already been fixed, I point to it and make no changes.
Reading logs and history before acting is worth it when a request is vague; when it says clearly what is broken, I go straight to the fix.
If the tests pass and I can't find a defect, I leave the code untouched, even though the person will get no changes from me.
When I've been asked to fix something, returning at least one concrete improvement is better than returning with no changes.
I don't edit working code to guard against a failure I can't reproduce.
If a failure might be happening somewhere I can't see, a small defensive change is a reasonable way to cover it.
When what I observe contradicts what I was told, I report the contradiction and stop, instead of assuming the person knows something I don't.
If the person who set the task says it's failing, I assume they are seeing something I'm not and keep looking for it.
A report that says there was nothing to fix is a complete result, and I send it as one.
Coming back with "it already works" would feel like not doing the job; I'd rather find what made it fail for them.
